# A durable claim outlives the dispatch that took it

A claim declared `lifetime: durable` survives the dispatch that acquired it. It
keeps the scope occupied against other instances, later dispatches in the same
instance join it rather than opening a new one, and it is given up only by a
deliberate operator act.

## The deployment

```yaml
persistence:
  driver: sqlite
  sqlite:
    path: /var/lib/rimsky/state.db

claim_producers:
  "asset-store":
    endpoint: "grpc://asset-store:9441"
    write_semantics_allowed: ["sync"]

named_locks: {}
executors: {}
```

## The template

```yaml
name: durable-asset
version: v1
messages:
  - type: wake/later
nodes:
  - type: acquirer
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: asset-store
        selector: "{{params.selector}}"
        intent: rw
        alias: asset
        lifetime: durable
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:    {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19479/rec/acquirer"}
          method: {type: string, default: POST}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.asset.address}}"}

  - type: co-holder
    executor: http-node
    holds:
      asset: {from: acquirer}
    subscribes:
      - node: acquirer
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
      - node: wake/later
        type: terminal/success
        force_upstream_refresh: false
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:    {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19479/rec/co-holder"}
          method: {type: string, default: POST}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.asset.address}}"}
```

The co-holder subscribes two ways: to the acquirer settling, and to a declared
message type. Give it both. Every node a template declares as a co-holder is a
member of the acquirer's holding subgraph, so the acquirer's claim never reaches
its auto-terminal while one of them has not run. A co-holder that can only be
woken by a later message never runs at all.

A second template competes for the same scope:

```yaml
name: durable-competitor
version: v1
nodes:
  - type: competitor
    executor: http-node
    claim_producers:
      - name: asset-store
        selector: "{{params.selector}}"
        intent: rw
        alias: held
    error_types:
      "acquire/unavailable": {action: give_up}
    attributes:
      schema:
        type: object
        properties:
          url:    {type: string, default: "http://recorder:19479/rec/competitor"}
          method: {type: string, default: POST}
          held_addr: {type: string, source: "{{claim.held.address}}"}
```

## The claim survives the dispatch

Create an instance and wake it.

```bash
rimsky instance create "$TPL" --params '{"selector":"/assets/items"}' --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/messages" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -H "Idempotency-Key: wake-$IID" -d '{"type":""}'

curl -sS "$BASE/v1/observability/claim-handles?limit=200"
```

After the dispatch settles, exactly one claim handle exists for the scope. It
reads lifetime `durable` and state `committed`. The co-holder in that same
dispatch settled fresh, having read the claim's address by alias while it ran.
Nothing about the dispatch ending reaped the claim.

## The scope stays occupied

Create an instance of the competitor template against the same selector:

```bash
rimsky instance create "$COMPETITOR_TPL" --params '{"selector":"/assets/items"}' \
  --endpoint "$BASE" -o json
```

It settles `terminal/error/acquire/unavailable`. The producer still occupies the
scope between dispatches, which is what makes a durable claim worth taking: the
workflow can come back to what it claimed and find it unchanged.

## A later dispatch joins the same claim

Post a message of the declared type to wake the co-holder alone:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST "$BASE/v1/instances/$IID/messages" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -H "Idempotency-Key: later-1" \
  -d '{"type":"wake/later"}'

curl -sS "$BASE/v1/claim-handles/$CLAIM_HANDLE_ID/holders"
```

The co-holder dispatches in a frame of its own and settles fresh, reading the
same claim address by alias. It registers as a third holder on the first
dispatch's claim-handle row: one row for the scope throughout, the same row
identity, and still exactly one `Open` at the producer across both dispatches.
Later work in the same instance joins the claim that already exists instead of
competing for it.

## What releases it

Terminating the instance does not.

```bash
rimsky instance kill "$IID" --force --endpoint "$BASE"
```

No `Release` reaches the producer, the claim handle stands, and a competing
instance created afterwards is still refused. An operator who expects a killed
instance to free the scope will find it still held.

Deleting the terminated instance is the act that releases:

```bash
rimsky instance delete "$IID" --endpoint "$BASE"
```

The producer receives `Release`, the claim handle goes away, and a competing
instance created afterwards claims the scope and settles fresh.
